power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A power analysis for parameter estimation was conducted on an online pwrSEM tool (Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021) to determine the required sample size for detecting a mediated effect of children's reading behaviour and reading motivation. Factor loadings for each of the three latent variables (home literacy environment, reading motivation, and reading comprehension) were set to .60 as requirement of an acceptable factor loading. Effect sizes based on previous literature were set to .27 -.32 (Dong et al, 2020; van der Sande et al, 2023). Results indicated that a sample size of 200 would yield approximately 85% power to detect a small mediation effect.
table.header: Power Analysis

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p>.05", "p = .051"), Sentence = c("The two groups did not differ on background characteristics (i.e. parental education, reading ability, and vocabulary) and reading behaviours and reading motivation at age 12.5, p>.05.", "Final model examining the longitudinal association between the home literacy environment, reading behaviour, reading motivation and reading comprehension Note: Indirect effect: .08, p = .02; Total effect: .34, p = .006; Reading comprehension R² = .31; Reading motivation R² = .07; Time spent reading R² = .62. ^ p = .051." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: The pre-registration of the hypotheses, analysis plan and analysis scripts are available on the OSF (https://osf.io/jvg94/overview).
text.formatted: The pre-registration of the hypotheses, analysis plan and analysis scripts are available on the OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/jvg94/overview">https://osf.io/jvg94/overview</ref>).

text.text: Data are available on the UK measuring the home literacy environment (HLE).

In addition to providing a novel five-year longitudinal test of the age-related drop in reading behaviour and motivation, our analyses specify precise mechanisms that link reading engagement, reading motivation, reading proficiency and HLE, as readers move from childhood to adolescence.
There is wide variation in terminology used to describe people's reading engagement and motivation (Conradi et al., 2014).
text.formatted: There is wide variation in terminology used to describe people's reading engagement and motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Conradi et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Reading engagement can be defined as a multidimensional construct distinguishing between children's reading behaviours, cognitive effort during reading, emotional response to what is read, and participation in reading activities with others (McGeown & Conradi, 2023).
text.formatted: Reading engagement can be defined as a multidimensional construct distinguishing between children's reading behaviours, cognitive effort during reading, emotional response to what is read, and participation in reading activities with others <ref type="bibr">(McGeown & Conradi, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, as in the present study, the majority of studies focus on children's reading behaviours, typically indexed in research through the frequency of reading different types of reading materials per day or per month assessed through questionnaires or diary measures (e.g. Lee et al., 2021; Mullis et al., 2006).
text.formatted: However, as in the present study, the majority of studies focus on children's reading behaviours, typically indexed in research through the frequency of reading different types of reading materials per day or per month assessed through questionnaires or diary measures (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lee et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mullis et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Well-established frameworks of reading motivation distinguish between intrinsic (reading for internal purposes) and extrinsic (reading for external rewards or recognition) drivers for reading (see Gurthrie & Wigfield, 2000), often based on broader frameworks of motivation, such as self-determination theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000).
text.formatted: Well-established frameworks of reading motivation distinguish between intrinsic (reading for internal purposes) and extrinsic (reading for external rewards or recognition) drivers for reading (see <ref type="bibr">Gurthrie & Wigfield, 2000)</ref>, often based on broader frameworks of motivation, such as self-determination theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Ryan & Deci, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Only a small number of longitudinal studies have examined changes in reading engagement or motivation.

In relation to reading engagement, Ulvinen et al. (2024)for instance tracked reading behaviours from age 7 to 15 years (n = 2525) in Finland, showing that individual differences in reading frequency were highly stable over time.
text.formatted: In relation to reading engagement, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ulvinen et al. (2024)</ref>for instance tracked reading behaviours from age 7 to 15 years (n = 2525) in Finland, showing that individual differences in reading frequency were highly stable over time.

text.text: Indeed, infrequent readers remained the most infrequent readers across the longitudinal study.
Additionally, from age 9 to 12 years, Becker and McElvany (2018) showed little change in reading frequency in a German sample (n = 772).
text.formatted: Additionally, from age 9 to 12 years, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Becker and McElvany (2018)</ref> showed little change in reading frequency in a German sample (n = 772).

text.text: Specifically, a small increase was observed for girls but none for boys.

For motivation, Retelsdorf et al. (2024) examined change in several aspects of reading motivation over time in 1508 German students from age 10 to 14/15 years, distinguishing between habitual reading for enjoyment or interest, and situational enjoyment of reading specific texts, in this case texts selected as part of school-based reading assessments.
text.formatted: For motivation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Retelsdorf et al. (2024)</ref> examined change in several aspects of reading motivation over time in 1508 German students from age 10 to 14/15 years, distinguishing between habitual reading for enjoyment or interest, and situational enjoyment of reading specific texts, in this case texts selected as part of school-based reading assessments.

text.text: They found all aspects of reading motivation declined from age 10 onwards, but this trend stabilised from age 13 to 14/15 years.
Similarly, Miyamoto et al. (2020) showed in a large longitudinal study in 6112 German students there was a decline in intrinsic motivation from age 10 to 15/16 years.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Miyamoto et al. (2020)</ref> showed in a large longitudinal study in 6112 German students there was a decline in intrinsic motivation from age 10 to 15/16 years.

text.text: Female students, from higher SES backgrounds and on the academic track in the German school system showed higher levels of reading motivation over time, where SES differences remained stable, but sex differences between male and female students increased over time.

A similar decline in intrinsic motivation to read outside of school was found in a small number of longitudinal studies with 175 Croatian students age 10 to 14 years (Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014) and 772 German students from age 9 to 12 years (Becker & McElvany, 2018).
text.formatted: A similar decline in intrinsic motivation to read outside of school was found in a small number of longitudinal studies with 175 Croatian students age 10 to 14 years <ref type="bibr">(Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014)</ref> and 772 German students from age 9 to 12 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Becker & McElvany, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In both studies, female students were more motivated to read than male students, but there was no widening of the gap over time.

Overall, these longitudinal studies reveal similar patterns as the cross-sectional National Literacy Trust (Clark et al., 2026) survey data suggests for reading enjoyment in the UK context, where children and young people's motivation seems to become lower with age and girls show higher levels of reading motivation than boys (Clark et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Overall, these longitudinal studies reveal similar patterns as the cross-sectional National Literacy Trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark et al., 2026)</ref> survey data suggests for reading enjoyment in the UK context, where children and young people's motivation seems to become lower with age and girls show higher levels of reading motivation than boys <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Clark et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence for changes in reading behaviours is more sparse and therefore more difficult to generalise.
Our study therefore addresses this important gap by examining within-person change in both reading behaviour and reading motivation across different demographic characteristics.

Previous research has shown that reading motivation is associated with how much time children and young people spend reading (Becker et al., 2010; Guthrie & Wigfield, 2000; Schiefele et al., 2012) and reading comprehension outcomes (Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014; McBreen & Savage, 2021; Mol & Bus, 2011), particularly when comparing students of different reading abilities (e.g. Qian et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that reading motivation is associated with how much time children and young people spend reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Becker et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Guthrie & Wigfield, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Schiefele et al., 2012)</ref> and reading comprehension outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">McBreen & Savage, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Mol & Bus, 2011)</ref>, particularly when comparing students of different reading abilities (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Qian et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: That is, according to theoretical frameworks such as the reading engagement model, comprehension of texts is not solely dependent on cognitive ability but is also shaped by motivational factors (Wigfield et al., 2008; Wigfield, 2016).
text.formatted: That is, according to theoretical frameworks such as the reading engagement model, comprehension of texts is not solely dependent on cognitive ability but is also shaped by motivational factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wigfield et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wigfield, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Whilst fundamental skills such as word decoding and vocabulary are important foundations, a person's motivation to read ultimately determines whether they will actively and willingly engage with texts (Cartwright et al, 2016; Schiefele et al, 2016).
text.formatted: Whilst fundamental skills such as word decoding and vocabulary are important foundations, a person's motivation to read ultimately determines whether they will actively and willingly engage with texts <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cartwright et al, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schiefele et al, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, it seems that intrinsic drivers are most strongly associated with subsequent reading and education outcomes (Becker et al., 2010; Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014).
text.formatted: More specifically, it seems that intrinsic drivers are most strongly associated with subsequent reading and education outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Becker et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, a longitudinal study from age 9 to 12 years showed that intrinsic reading motivation at age 10 was associated with a composite measure of vocabulary, decoding and reading comprehension two years later (Becker et al., 2010).
text.formatted: For instance, a longitudinal study from age 9 to 12 years showed that intrinsic reading motivation at age 10 was associated with a composite measure of vocabulary, decoding and reading comprehension two years later <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Becker et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This association was mediated by reading behaviour.
Children who showed higher intrinsic motivation for reading also reported to read more and showed higher levels of reading ability.

Similarly, Torppa et al. (2020) showed positive associations between reading behaviours and later reading comprehension skills from age 9 to 16 years, where more time spent reading was associated with better reading comprehension skills.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Torppa et al. (2020)</ref> showed positive associations between reading behaviours and later reading comprehension skills from age 9 to 16 years, where more time spent reading was associated with better reading comprehension skills.

text.text: In addition to child characteristics such as sex or reading proficiency, the home environment also plays a role in shaping children's engagement with reading.
The home literacy model (Sénéchal 2006; Sénéchal & LeFevre, 2002) emphasises the role of early home experiences in shaping both children's cognitive skills and their motivation for reading.
text.formatted: The home literacy model <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sénéchal 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sénéchal & LeFevre, 2002)</ref> emphasises the role of early home experiences in shaping both children's cognitive skills and their motivation for reading.

text.text: This model has been supported by a number of previous research examining various aspects of the home literacy environment including parent educational level (Chen et al, 2018), socioeconomic status (Michael & Kyriakides, 2023), parental support (Klauda, 2009), and parental beliefs about the importance of reading (Baker & Scher, 2002).
text.formatted: This model has been supported by a number of previous research examining various aspects of the home literacy environment including parent educational level <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chen et al, 2018)</ref>, socioeconomic status <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Michael & Kyriakides, 2023)</ref>, parental support <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Klauda, 2009)</ref>, and parental beliefs about the importance of reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baker & Scher, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: These factors are argued to contribute to both the quality and frequency of reading interactions at home, which in turn influence reading motivation and later language achievement (i.e. Sénéchal 2006).
text.formatted: These factors are argued to contribute to both the quality and frequency of reading interactions at home, which in turn influence reading motivation and later language achievement (i.e. <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Sénéchal 2006</ref>).

text.text: An important gap in this research is that it has focused primarily on early reading development, but the home environment likely still plays an important role in shaping attitudes toward reading beyond this developmental period.

As in younger children, seeing others reading, being exposed to positive beliefs and encouragement, and availability of books are positively associated with young people's reading behaviours and motivation (Klauda, 2009).
text.formatted: As in younger children, seeing others reading, being exposed to positive beliefs and encouragement, and availability of books are positively associated with young people's reading behaviours and motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Klauda, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Van Steensel and Jongerling (2025) found in a cross-sectional study with 5751 Dutch students across primary and secondary years reporting on perceptions of parent support and reading motivation, that parent support was associated with extrinsic and intrinsic reading motivation across childhood.
A more stimulating home literacy environment provided by parents was associated with higher levels of intrinsic reading motivation, and this association was stronger for the adolescence age group.
Moreover, this influence of the home environment can have long lasting influences on young people's reading ability and reading motivation.

In their longitudinal study with 198 Finnish children followed from age 2 to 15 years, Torppa et al. (2022) found early literacy activities before starting school, such as shared reading, were associated with reading motivation at age 8/9 and reading comprehension ability at age 15.
text.formatted: In their longitudinal study with 198 Finnish children followed from age 2 to 15 years, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Torppa et al. (2022)</ref> found early literacy activities before starting school, such as shared reading, were associated with reading motivation at age 8/9 and reading comprehension ability at age 15.

text.text: Whilst these studies seem to suggest that the early or concurrent home literacy environment is associated with reading motivation and reading outcomes, it's unclear whether this association is best explained by an indirect mechanism (the home literacy environment shaping young people's motivation for reading, leading to more time spent reading), or whether there is a direct benefit to having a more stimulating home literacy environment which supports young people's reading comprehension abilities, regardless of whether they read independently themselves (for example, by supporting the types of conversations held or the quality of overheard speech in the family home).

The present study we aimed to: 1) provide a novel longitudinal test of the decline in reading behaviour and reading motivation in middle childhood and early adolescence across eight time points; and 2) examine the role of the home literacy environment, reading behaviour and motivation in young people's reading comprehension skills.

Data from a longitudinal study (n = 598) in [Blinded] in the United Kingdom was used to answer the following research questions: 1) How does reading behaviour and reading motivation change from age 10-15?
text.formatted: Data from a longitudinal study (n = 598) in <ref type="bibr">[Blinded]</ref> in the United Kingdom was used to answer the following research questions: 1) How does reading behaviour and reading motivation change from age 10-15?

text.text: Based on previous longitudinal and concurrent research discussed above, we hypothesised that young people's reading behaviour (time spent reading outside of school), and reading motivation decline with age.

We know that person and environment characteristics as sex and socioeconomic status are also associated with differences in reading engagement and reading motivation, where there are concerns of male students engaging less with reading than female students (Clark & Teravainen, 2017), and children and young people from lower SES backgrounds engaging less with reading than those from higher SES backgrounds (Miyamoto et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We know that person and environment characteristics as sex and socioeconomic status are also associated with differences in reading engagement and reading motivation, where there are concerns of male students engaging less with reading than female students <ref type="bibr">(Clark & Teravainen, 2017)</ref>, and children and young people from lower SES backgrounds engaging less with reading than those from higher SES backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Miyamoto et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We will therefore control for these in our analyses.

2) Does the home literacy environment directly affect reading proficiency in middle childhood and early adolescence, or is this mediated by young people's own motivation for reading and reading behaviour?

We hypothesised that a positive home literacy environment will positively influence young people's reading motivation, leading to more spent time reading, which in turn positively benefits reading comprehension abilities.
Alternatively, young people's own motivation could be a protective factor for their reading development, when they come from backgrounds with a less encouraging home literacy environment.
In this case, a positive association between reading motivation, time spent reading and reading comprehension is expected, regardless of any effects of the home literacy environment.
The pre-registration of the hypotheses, analysis plan and analysis scripts are available on the OSF (https://osf.io/jvg94/overview?view_only=9bcc8914fa6d437599bf53f79082ad7f).
text.formatted: The pre-registration of the hypotheses, analysis plan and analysis scripts are available on the OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/jvg94/overview?view_only=9bcc8914fa6d437599bf53f79082ad7f">https://osf.io/jvg94/overview?view_only=9bcc8914fa6d437599bf53f79082ad7f</ref>).

text.text: Data is available on the OSF: https://osf.io/jvg94/overview?
view_only=9bcc8914fa6d437599bf53f79082ad7f and included as supplementary files.

Participants were part of an existing study examining reading development from school entry at age 4 (Mage = 4.64, SD = .30 years; n = 788; 375 girls; see Authors (2020) for longitudinal analyses from age 4 to 9 years and Authors (2023) for analyses from age 10 to 13 years of reading and vocabulary development).
The time points included in the current analyses are data collected between June 2017 to June 2022.
In 2017, participants comprised 598 children age 10 (Mage = 10.29, SD = .29 years; 285 girls) attending Year 5 of primary education.
The following time points and demographic characteristics are presented in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The following time points and demographic characteristics are presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: At ages 10 and 11, participants attended 16 primary schools in suburban areas of [blinded].
text.formatted: At ages 10 and 11, participants attended 16 primary schools in suburban areas of <ref type="bibr">[blinded]</ref>.

text.text: From age 12, they were attending 53 secondary schools in the same area.

School-level data from primary schools indicated a broad range of socioeconomic backgrounds: Index of Multiple Deprivation deciles ranged from 1-10 (Noble et al., 2019), and the proportion within each school who were eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) ranged from 1% -48% (mean 18%).
At secondary, 16% of the participants were eligible for FSM.
At primary, 10% spoke English as an Additional Language (EAL); at secondary (final time point) this was 9%.
At each testing point, we worked with all participants from the ongoing study for whom we had parental consent and pupil assent.
There was substantial attrition between ages 10 and 11, this was due to the introduction of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) that required new written consent from parents at age 11.
The large attrition after age 13.5 (October 2020) was caused by school closures during the global pandemic.
Notably, attrition was typically at the whole school level, where attrition was mainly due to school access and not individual withdrawal from the study.
We compared the participants who were retained in the study after age 13.5 to the participants who no longer took part after this time point to check for attrition bias.
The two groups did not differ on background characteristics (i.e. parental education, reading ability, and vocabulary) and reading behaviours and reading motivation at age 12.5, p>.05.
text.formatted: The two groups did not differ on background characteristics (i.e. parental education, reading ability, and vocabulary) and reading behaviours and reading motivation at age 12.5, p>.05.

Timeline longitudinal study.
Age 10-15 time points are included in the current analyses.

A power analysis for parameter estimation was conducted on an online pwrSEM tool (Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021) to determine the required sample size for detecting a mediated effect of children's reading behaviour and reading motivation.
text.formatted: A power analysis for parameter estimation was conducted on an online pwrSEM tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021)</ref> to determine the required sample size for detecting a mediated effect of children's reading behaviour and reading motivation.

text.text: Factor loadings for each of the three latent variables (home literacy environment, reading motivation, and reading comprehension) were set to .60 as requirement of an acceptable factor loading.
Effect sizes based on previous literature were set to .27 -.32 (Dong et al, 2020; van der Sande et al, 2023).
text.formatted: Effect sizes based on previous literature were set to .27 -.32 <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dong et al, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">van der Sande et al, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Results indicated that a sample size of 200 would yield approximately 85% power to detect a small mediation effect.
Reading Literacy Study (Martin et al., 2007) student questionnaire was used to measure children's reading behaviour and reading motivation from age 10-15.
text.formatted: Reading Literacy Study <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Martin et al., 2007)</ref> student questionnaire was used to measure children's reading behaviour and reading motivation from age 10-15.

text.text: Reading behaviour:
Children were asked how often they read different types of reading materials on a 4-point rating scale ranging from "never" to "everyday".

We included only questions about the time spent reading (novels or books) outside of school: 'How much time do you spend reading outside of school', 'How often do you read for fun', 'How often do you read stories or novels?'
Reading motivation: Children were then asked to rate statements regarding reading motivation on a 4-point rating scale ranging from "disagree a lot" to "agree a lot".
Example questions included: "I enjoy reading", "I would like more time for reading", and "I only read if I have to".
We used the reading enjoyment questions from the PIRLS questionnaire to form a single factor indicating young people's motivation for reading.
At age 12.5, children read one fiction and one non-fiction passage from the York Assessment of Reading for Comprehension secondary school edition (YARC; Stothard et al., 2010).
text.formatted: At age 12.5, children read one fiction and one non-fiction passage from the York Assessment of Reading for Comprehension secondary school edition (YARC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Stothard et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: To cover the range of ability, one of these was an easier passage (a non-fiction text designed for pupils aged 8-9) and one was harder (an ageappropriate fiction text).
The easier passage was read aloud and the harder passage was read silently.
After reading each passage, participants answered 13 open-ended questions that measured literal and inferential comprehension.
Cronbach's alpha for this sample was .70.

At the age 11 time point, a questionnaire was provided to the parents asking about early shared reading practices at home, parents' or carers' own reading behaviours and reading motivation and number of books in the home.
Example questions include, "About how many books are there in your home?"
and "When you are at home, how often do you read for your enjoyment?".
Parents were also asked to rate their own reading motivation on a 4-point rating scale ranging from "agree a lot" to "disagree a lot".
Example items include, "I read only if I have to", "reading is an important activity in my home", and "I like to spend my spare time reading".
Data was collected individually and on laptops at schools.
At each time point, tasks were administered in a fixed order, in one 45-minute session.
Reading tasks were administered individually by a trained research assistant, remaining tasks were administered on a laptop.
After the 2020 time points all tasks were completed on laptops, supervised by a trained research assistant or a teacher.

Linear mixed effects models were fitted to examine the trajectory of change in reading behaviour and reading motivation over time using the age 10-15 data, using the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Linear mixed effects models were fitted to examine the trajectory of change in reading behaviour and reading motivation over time using the age 10-15 data, using the lme4 package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator was used to fit the models.
The normality of residuals assumptions was checked for the reading behaviour and reading motivation models using qqplots.
To model the trajectory of change, linear, quadratic and cubic terms were added to the model.
The models included participant-level random effects.
Due to the large number of schools and only a small number of children per school, we did not include School-level random effects.
Model comparisons using the anova function were used to select the trajectory that best fits the data.
Finally, we tested if trajectories vary by sex (girls vs boys) and socioeconomic status (lower vs high).

Participants were classified as lower SES if mothers' highest qualification was A-level or lower (equivalent to a high school degree), resulting in a relatively even split 55% lower SES and 45% higher SES.

Confirmatory Factor Analysis was performed to test the factor structure for the following constructs: the home literacy environment (measured by books in the home, early literacy activities, parent/carer time spent reading, and parent/carer reading motivation), children's reading motivation (measured using eight items from the PIRLS questionnaire), reading behaviour (measured using three items from the PIRLS questionnaire related to time spent reading books or novels) and children's reading comprehension (measured by easy and difficult passage scores).
Identification was ensured by fixing the first loading of each latent variable to 1.
Following Brown (2015) acceptability was evaluated based on the following criteria: factor loadings need to be statistically significant p<.05 and standardised loadings need to be > .03.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Brown (2015)</ref> acceptability was evaluated based on the following criteria: factor loadings need to be statistically significant p<.05 and standardised loadings need to be > .03.

text.text: Modifications indices were used to assess strains in the model.

A mediation model was fitted within the Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) framework to test the whether the HLE directly predicted children's reading comprehension ability or via children's reading motivation and reading behaviour.
In all CFA and SEM models, model fit was evaluated using the following criteria: CFI > .90, TLI > .90, RMSEA < .08 (Brown, 2015).
text.formatted: In all CFA and SEM models, model fit was evaluated using the following criteria: CFI > .90, TLI > .90, RMSEA < .08 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brown, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The models contained ordered categorical data, therefore a mean-adjusted weighted least square estimator was used (WLSMV), using pairwise deletion to handle missing data.

To examine the trajectory of change in reading behaviour and reading motivation tested whether adding quadratic and cubic terms to the baseline linear model improved the fit to the data.
Adding a quadratic (c 2 (1) = 6.47, p =.01) and cubic (c 2 (1) = 9.54, p =.002) term improved the model fit, indicating that the change in reading behaviour followed a curvilinear pattern.
As can be seen in Figure 2, the time spent reading first declined, with the lowest point at age 13.5, with a small increase to age 14 and 15.

The present study aimed to: 1) provide a novel longitudinal test of within-person change in reading behaviour and reading motivation in middle childhood and early adolescence; and 2) examine how young people's reading motivation and reading behaviour are associated with later reading proficiency, and whether this is directly or indirectly influenced by their home literacy environment (HLE).
Our findings showed strongest declines in both reading behaviour and reading motivation from age 11 to 13 years, which stabilised at age 14-15.
The trajectories for both reading behaviour and reading motivation differed for boys and girls, as well as for higher vs lower socioeconomic (SES) backgrounds.

For the second aim we found that HLE influenced reading motivation both directly and indirectly: adolescents with a stronger reading motivation at 11.5-years-of-age in turn reported to read more in their own time and performed better on our reading comprehension measure at age 12.5 years.

Turning to age-related changes in behaviour and motivation first, the decline in reading behaviour and reading motivation is in line with previous cross-sectional reports on age-related differences in these constructs (Clark et al., 2026), and the small number of longitudinal studies with these age groups (Miyamoto et al., 2020; Retelsdorf et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Turning to age-related changes in behaviour and motivation first, the decline in reading behaviour and reading motivation is in line with previous cross-sectional reports on age-related differences in these constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark et al., 2026)</ref>, and the small number of longitudinal studies with these age groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Miyamoto et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Retelsdorf et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, in line with Retelsdorf et al. (2023) our study also shows that this decline is most prominent from age 11 to 13 years.
text.formatted: Interestingly, in line with <ref type="bibr">Retelsdorf et al. (2023)</ref> our study also shows that this decline is most prominent from age 11 to 13 years.

text.text: This could potentially reflect changes in priorities or reasons for reading.

Between 11 to 13-years-of-age is a time when children in the UK transition from primary to secondary education, which may change their priorities and focus whilst they adjust to their new school environment and increasing independence and autonomy over their own time (e.g. Jindal-Snape et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Between 11 to 13-years-of-age is a time when children in the UK transition from primary to secondary education, which may change their priorities and focus whilst they adjust to their new school environment and increasing independence and autonomy over their own time (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Jindal-Snape et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This is also a time in which peer influences become more and more important, and views towards reading may also change (e.g. reading may not be a socially acceptable activity; Webber et al., 2024) or when the type of reading they engage with shifts.
text.formatted: This is also a time in which peer influences become more and more important, and views towards reading may also change (e.g. reading may not be a socially acceptable activity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Webber et al., 2024)</ref> or when the type of reading they engage with shifts.

text.text: For instance, previous research with this age group shows young people indicate to read for many different reasons.

Adolescents report to read for learning or for wellbeing reasons, such as reading for managing difficult emotions or relaxation (Clark et al., 2026), but our questionnaire did not include questions about these topics.
text.formatted: Adolescents report to read for learning or for wellbeing reasons, such as reading for managing difficult emotions or relaxation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark et al., 2026)</ref>, but our questionnaire did not include questions about these topics.

text.text: They also indicate to prefer different modalities for different types of reading.

For instance, some indicate to prefer paper when reading narrative fiction and non-fiction, whereas phones are the preferred modality to read social media, news, fanfiction or comics (Loh & Sun, 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, some indicate to prefer paper when reading narrative fiction and non-fiction, whereas phones are the preferred modality to read social media, news, fanfiction or comics <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Loh & Sun, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Our data captures reading of books and novels and general motivation for reading (e.g. reading for enjoyment, talking about books, reading to imagine other worlds), but may not fully capture the full range or reading behaviours and motivations for reading that are relevant within this age group.
Importantly, the findings for sex and SES indicate that the change in reading behaviour and reading motivation differs for boys and girls and for higher and lower SES groups.

Whilst overall, our data suggest the decline stabilises at age 14, when examining trajectories separately for boys and girls, we can see that rather than trajectories levelling off, the trajectories diverge for boys and girls in our study.
The most prominent pattern is of an increase in reading behaviours and reading motivation for girls from age 13.5 years onwards, contrasting with an ongoing decline for boys.
These findings resonate with wider concerns around boys engaging less with volitional reading than girls (Jabbar & Warreich, 2023; McGeown, 2015; Steinmann & Strietholt, 2025).
text.formatted: These findings resonate with wider concerns around boys engaging less with volitional reading than girls <ref type="bibr">(Jabbar & Warreich, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">McGeown, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Steinmann & Strietholt, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The SES related differences on the other hand, seem to be mostly due to a stronger decline in reading behaviour and reading motivation for the higher SES group after age 12.5 years.
Unlike previous studies, that only followed young people up to age 12 (Becker & McElvany, 2018) or 14 (Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014), our data shows that group differences can emerge after this age.
text.formatted: Unlike previous studies, that only followed young people up to age 12 <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Becker & McElvany, 2018)</ref> or 14 <ref type="bibr">(Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014)</ref>, our data shows that group differences can emerge after this age.

text.text: This highlights the importance of following reading motivations and reading behaviours across childhood and adolescence to gain a better understanding of how reading behaviours and reading motivation change across different individual characteristics and backgrounds and what implications this might have for policy and intervention.

The role of the home environment in reading behaviours, motivation and reading outcomes As for the second aim, examining the role of the HLE in young people's reading behaviours, motivation and ability, our findings showed that both the HLE and young people's own reading motivation and reading behaviours were associated with their subsequent reading comprehension abilities.
Young people from richer home literacy environments reported higher levels of reading motivation, more leisure reading and performed better on the reading comprehension measure.

This supports well established findings on the importance of HLE for reading motivation and reading attainments (Dong et al., 2020; Mol & Bus, 2011) and we build on this to demonstrate two novel aspects of this relationship.
text.formatted: This supports well established findings on the importance of HLE for reading motivation and reading attainments <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dong et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Mol & Bus, 2011)</ref> and we build on this to demonstrate two novel aspects of this relationship.

text.text: First, that the importance of HLE is longer lived than often thought.

Although effects of HLE may be most obvious in early childhood (when children are wholly dependent on caregivers for their reading experiences), our findings show that even in middle childhood when children are reading independently, the home literacy environment is important in shaping young people's motivation for reading.
Second, we uncover the mechanisms by which HLE, motivation and comprehension are associated and demonstrate both indirect and direct effects of HLE on reading comprehension.

As expected, even in middle childhood, when most have become proficient readers and gain more autonomy over what they read and how they spend their free time, the HLE plays a vital role in shaping young people's reading motivation and encouraging reading.

This could be due to a continuing and cumulative effects of parents and carers providing access to reading materials, modelling their own reading behaviours and early shared reading throughout childhood, but also shaping their children's values and interests more broadly (Klauda, 2009).
text.formatted: This could be due to a continuing and cumulative effects of parents and carers providing access to reading materials, modelling their own reading behaviours and early shared reading throughout childhood, but also shaping their children's values and interests more broadly <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Klauda, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, the HLE also shows a direct influence on comprehension ability, potentially due to the quality or quantity of language exposure (Mol & Bus, 2011), support provided by parents or carers for literacy related-activities (Dong et al., 2020; Claes et al., 2024), or perhaps this could reflect heritable components of parents own reading proficiency that we did not capture in our study (Hart et al., 2021; van Bergen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Yet, the HLE also shows a direct influence on comprehension ability, potentially due to the quality or quantity of language exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Mol & Bus, 2011)</ref>, support provided by parents or carers for literacy related-activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dong et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Claes et al., 2024)</ref>, or perhaps this could reflect heritable components of parents own reading proficiency that we did not capture in our study <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hart et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">van Bergen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings on the role of HLE have important implications for intervention and policy, emphasising volitional reading is not just something that should be encouraged in schools, but there is a role for parents and carers in providing an encouraging environment for reading in the home.
We focused our longitudinal analyses of reading behaviours on time spent reading books or novels.

This was based on previous research that shows book reading is the strongest driver for subsequent reading and vocabulary development, compared to other reading materials (Pfost & Heyne, 2023; Torppa et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This was based on previous research that shows book reading is the strongest driver for subsequent reading and vocabulary development, compared to other reading materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Pfost & Heyne, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Torppa et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, modelling changes in different types of reading young people engage in, such as non-fiction reading, online reading or reading comics could still provide a more complete picture of how reading behaviours change in middle childhood and adolescence.

Whilst they might be less predictive of reading and vocabulary ability, young people report to read for many different reasons (Clark et al., 2024; Webbet er al., 2023) and reading experiences and types of reading for instance are also found to differ by sex or gender (Clark et al., 2024 McGeown, 2015).

text.text: Research in early and middle childhood shows that both parent's own reading ability and home literacy environment, as assessed by the number of books in the home, are associated with children's reading skills (van Bergen et al, 2017).

text.text: Our measure of the home literacy environment does not allow us to tease apart any heritable characteristics and specific influences of the home environment, as we for instance did not assess parents' reading ability (i.e. Hart et al., 2021).

text.text: Finally, there was a large drop in participant numbers due to difficulty accessing schools during the global 2020-2021 pandemic.

There is therefore a risk that the effects of sex and SES on reading motivation and behaviour trajectories are specific to the sample retained after age 12.5 years whose characteristics may not generalise.
However, the differences in trajectories for this age group are unlikely to be easily explained by specific characteristics of a subsample.
The pattern we found was complex, with an ongoing decline for boys alongside an increase for girls, alongside a stronger decline for the higher SES group.

Nevertheless, to explore this possibility, we tested whether the smaller sample that continued to participate after age 12.5 years was still a good representation of the full sample (i.e. ensure not only higher SES schools or avid readers were retained in the study).

The sample that remained during the pandemic did not differ in background characteristics or in reading motivation and reading behaviour at an earlier time point, meaning that the smaller sample retained in the study was still a good representation of the full sample.
We found declines in reading behaviour and reading motivation that were most prominent from age 11 to 13 years.

In the UK, this is a time when students transition to secondary and adjust to a new school environment and responsibilities, if also often coincides with more autonomy over how they spend their own time.
Importantly, our study shows reading behaviour and motivation increased for girls after this age, but not for boys.
Our findings also emphasise the importance of regular reading of books and novels outside of school for reading proficiency.
The significant contribution of the HLE indicates that encouraging reading is not just school's responsibility.
Parents own attitudes towards reading, their own reading behaviours and shared reading in early literacy development help shape children's reading motivation and reading behaviour.
